name: Westside San Joaquin drip block
headline: No rain from May to October. Water deliveries swing from full to zero, so half the ground sits idle.
story: A 155-acre block near Five Points grows processing tomatoes on buried drip, then sits idle the following year because there is not enough water to farm every acre. Surface-water allocations collapse in dry years, groundwater pumping is capped under the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, and salts build in the clay loam. The question is what can earn something on the idle year using winter rain and very little irrigation, while giving tomatoes the disease break they need.

irrigation.label: Subsurface drip, district water plus wells

baseline_rotation.name: Processing tomato - idle year
baseline_rotation.note: The Cropland Data Layer shows tomatoes alternating with idle years on this block (tomato 2021, idle 2022, tomato 2023; chickpea in 2020). Edit the baseline to match your block.

water_context.aquifer: San Joaquin Valley aquifer system (Westside subbasin)
water_context.in_situ_source: California DWR periodic groundwater-level measurements, Westside subbasin (drought-period declines; partial recovery in wet years)
water_context.note: Subsidence along this corridor has damaged canals. Groundwater sustainability plans set pumping allocations that tighten through 2040.

tomato.note: Canneries contract acreage each winter; no contract, no crop.

cotton.note: Gins remain, though acreage and gin numbers have fallen.

winter_wheat.note: Dairies buy wheat as silage or grain; flexible outlet.

triticale.note: Dairy silage demand is strong throughout the valley.

safflower.note: Oilseed contracts are available some years; confirm before planting.

chickpea.note: Garbanzo handlers contract on the westside; price swings are large.

alfalfa.note: Dairy hay demand is strong, but alfalfa is the thirstiest option.
